The Cairo population development map gives us the compass, rights, choice, dignity. That is the filter through which every policy, every digital health initiative, every AI governance decision must pass. That is why this commission matters. Thank you, UN DESA. Thank you, all regional economic commission. Thank you, WHO. Thank you, UNESCO. Thank you, ITU. Multilateral negotiation are difficult. Reaching consensus on issues that touch the most intimate dimension of human life is never easy, some years impossible, just like this one. And yet, we keep showing up. My 5,000 UNFPA colleagues, on behalf of them and myself, we are very grateful to all of you. The Minister of Finance of a country told me yesterday, "I am not sure people realize the true force and support UNFPA provide to people in countries." Everything we do does not end up on social media as it is so intimate when it is about people's life, maternal health, maternal morbidity, GBV, or it is so confidential when it is about data, census, as it is the very indicators and information for good governance. So allow me to recognize the effort of delegation, all of you, who engage diligently in the true spirit of multilateralism. Thank you for the negotiating good faith, even where position diverged. That is why it is so unfortunate that consensus on an intergovernmental outcome on this special theme could not be reached this year. But the absence of final document does not diminish the urgency of this agenda or the importance of this commission. the only dedicated space in the United Nation where we can discuss population issues, rights, and development. I thank the Executive Director of the United Nations Population Fund, the Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs, Madam Executive Director of the UNFPA, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, delegates, As we conclude the 59th session of the Commission on Population and Development, I would like to briefly go back to reflect on the substance of our discussions and on the broader significance of our work. This session has reaffirmed the continued relevance of the Program of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development as the normative foundation of policies on population and development. More than three decades after its adoption, the Program of Action continues to guide our efforts to advance health, rights, and sustainable development in an increasingly complex and rapidly changing world. For the first time, the Commission examined the intersection between population, technology, and research as a specific standalone theme. That discussion could not have been more timely in a context of accelerating technological change that is reshaping societies, economies, and demographic dynamics Our deliberations have highlighted both the challenges we face, particularly with regard to inequalities, access, and safeguards, as well as the wide range of opportunities that technology and research offer to accelerate progress, strengthen evidence-based policymaking, and ensure that no one is left behind. The exchanges that took place during this session have provided valuable insights into how technological innovation can support the implementation of the ICPD Programme of Action, while underscoring the importance of inclusive, equitable, rights-based approaches. These reflections will remain relevant as we approach the 2027 SDG Summit and beyond. At the same time, I regret that Despite the considerable efforts made by the co-facilitators and all the members of the Bureau, including through extensive informal consultations and bilateral exchanges, it was not possible to reach consensus on a final document for this session. However, this outcome in no way diminishes the value of the substantive discussions that we have had, nor the commitment demonstrated by delegations throughout the process. The Commission on Population and Development remains the only intergovernmental forum where countries come together to review issues, programs, and policies at the intersection of demographic change, development, human rights, and gender equality. The absence of consensus on certain issues is not a failure, but rather a reminder of the enduring importance of this Commission as a unique forum for dialogue, knowledge sharing, and sustained multilateral engagement on matters that affect all of our societies. Our inability to overcome our differences and reach consensus over the past four weeks must not lead us to withdraw into isolation or abandon the valuable global dialogue fostered by the CPD.
